new_statements.quote: The few statements that can be made about the vocalization of Ancient South Arabian are based on the use of the glides w and y. [...] Apart from these few hints, practically nothing is known about the vocalization of the Ancient South Arabian texts preserved for us. The question of a possible differentiation of syllables according to vowel quantity, therefore, likewise cannot be answered with certainty, nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress location can be stated: Qatabanic (like all Ancient South Arabian) is attested only in unvocalized consonantal script with no reading tradition, and the primary description says explicitly that no conclusions about accent are possible. This is a first-hand 'accent unknowable' statement, not a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only stress-related remark anywhere in the ASA literature opened is Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224, a speculation that Minaic 'parasitic h' reflects 'a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)' -- Minaic, not Qatabanic.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the whole Ancient South Arabian epigraphic corpus (four dialects incl. Qatabanic), not about word vs phrase domain; no citation forms exist (dead epigraphic language).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Nebes & Stein 2004) is made for Ancient South Arabian as a whole (Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic; chapter p. 454 names Qatabanic explicitly as one of the four dialects covered); it is not Qatabanic-specific. The same passage was used by sibling audits for hadr1235 (Hadramitic) and saba1279 (Sabaic). Qatabanic is an extinct epigraphic language (c. 7th c. BC - 2nd c. AD) written only in the unvocalized consonantal musnad script with no reading tradition, so no first-hand location of word stress can exist.

sources.citation: Kogan, Leonid E. & Andrey V. Korotayev. 1997. 'Sayhadic (Epigraphic South Arabian)'. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 220-241. London: Routledge.
sources.note: p. 223: 'Since the South Arabian system of writing is purely consonantal, we cannot draw any direct information about Sayhadic vowels.' No stress section; only mention (p. 224) is speculation that Minaic parasitic h 'was caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)' -- Minaic only, nothing on Qatabanian.
